source: Langley (1979) Rediscovering physics with BACON.3 (IJCAI); abstract via search result only
finding: BACON.3 is a data-driven discovery program. It rediscovered versions of the ideal gas law, Kepler's third law, Coulomb's law, Ohm's law, and Galileo's pendulum and acceleration laws from tabulated data.
numbers: 6 laws rediscovered; no human comparison; noise-free or lightly noisy tables
limits: Only the abstract surfaced in search; full paper not read. Data were pre-selected variables, so the hard step of choosing which variables matter was done by the human.
agent_relevance: BACON is the template for a cheap, code-run hypothesis loop: propose a term, test if constant within error, else combine terms. This is a check that needs no model opinion (fits G3, G8).

source: Langley, Simon, Bradshaw, Zytkow (1987) Scientific Discovery: Computational Explorations of the Creative Processes (MIT Press); review text via search result only
finding: The book collects BACON, GLAUBER, STAHL, DALTON, DENDRAL-like and other programs. Reviews say they rediscovered laws named after Boyle, Ohm, Kepler, Coulomb, Snell, Black and Joule.
numbers: 7 named laws in review summary; core rule: if two terms rise together, test their ratio; if one rises while the other falls, test their product
limits: Book not opened. Benchmarks were historical cases chosen after the fact; a later philosophy critique says the two case studies (sine law, Kepler III) cannot show a general method.
agent_relevance: Gives named, tiny operators (ratio, product, intrinsic property) that code can apply and score. Candidate for a scripted open-mode operator list beside O1-O8.

source: Encyclopedia entry: Scientific Discovery, Computational Models of (Int. Encyclopedia of Social and Behavioral Sciences)
finding: Most discovery programs are recursive search over a space of expressions with a test of fit and heuristics to prune. BACON applies an INCREASING operator to P/D and P^2/D, finds P^2/D^3 constant (Kepler III). Almost all programs address theory formation; few model experiment design or turning raw data into evidence.
numbers: No measured effects. Notes some systems produced findings published in major journals (Valdes-Perez 1995).
quote: few systems have simulated or supported substantial experimental activities
limits: Review; claims about publishable findings are not quantified. Single-task systems are called poor imitations of human variety.
agent_relevance: Two spaces (hypotheses and data) searched together is a clean description of an open mode with a running check: each hypothesis dictates the data needed to test it.

source: Udrescu, Tegmark (2020) AI Feynman: a physics-inspired method for symbolic regression
finding: A symbolic regression system using symmetry, separability and dimensional analysis found all 100 Feynman-lecture equations. The best earlier public software (Eureqa) solved 71.
numbers: 100/100 vs 71/100; 100 equations from the Feynman Lectures; plus 20 harder 'bonus' equations in the paper
limits: Equations are textbook, clean data, and likely in training corpora of LLMs. Success depends on the equations having physics-like structure.
agent_relevance: BACON's modern descendant. Shows code-side decomposition (find symmetry, separate variables) beats raw search, a pattern an LLM agent can call as a tool.

source: Grayeli, Sehgal, Costilla-Reyes, Cranmer, Chaudhuri (2024) Symbolic regression with a learned concept library (LaSR)
finding: Adding an LLM that proposes and evolves natural-language concepts to a genetic symbolic-regression search raised exact solves on the 100 Feynman equations over plain PySR. Gains held even with a small open model (Llama3-8B).
numbers: Exact solves: PySR 59/100; LaSR Llama3-8B 67 (p=1%), 69 (p=5%), 71 (p=10%); LaSR GPT-3.5 72/100 (p=1%). p = fraction of LLM-driven operations.
limits: Feynman set is likely memorised by LLMs; ablations of concept library and variable names reduce gains. Single benchmark.
agent_relevance: Evidence that an LLM as a proposal operator inside a code-run search loop adds value over the search alone, and that more LLM calls (p) help monotonically here.

source: Shojaee, Meidani, Gupta, Farimani, Reddy (2024) LLM-SR: scientific equation discovery via programming with LLMs
finding: LLM-SR has the LLM write equation skeletons as Python functions, fits parameters by optimiser, and feeds the best back into the prompt. It beat symbolic regression baselines, most clearly out of domain.
numbers: Example: OOD NMSE 0.0037 for LLM-SR vs OOD NMSE > 1 for other methods (one oscillator problem); tested on physics, biology, material science problems
limits: Problems used well-known forms, so memorisation is possible (the follow-up c07 tests this). Numbers are from selected problems.
agent_relevance: A working model: LLM proposes, code fits and scores, scores go back into context. Matches 'code selects' (G5) and 'revise from real output' (G2).

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: a new benchmark for scientific equation discovery with LLMs
finding: Benchmark built to defeat memorisation: LSR-Transform rewrites known equations into unfamiliar forms; LSR-Synth makes new synthetic equations. The best system still solved under a third.
numbers: Best: 31.5% symbolic accuracy on LSR-Transform, 28.1% on LSR-Synth; example row GPT-4o-mini LLM-SR 31.53% SA on one subset; SA strongly correlates with numeric precision Acc0.1
limits: Symbolic accuracy judged by an LLM equivalence check; many methods and backbones compared, gaps small between methods.
agent_relevance: Strong warning: earlier LLM equation-discovery wins were partly recall. Our open mode must be tested on transformed, unfamiliar problems (G3).

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: towards data-driven discovery with LLMs
finding: Benchmark of data-driven hypothesis tasks drawn from published papers across 6 domains. All tested agent frameworks scored low.
numbers: Best system 25% (hypothesis match score). Domain split: economics 25%, sociology 23%, engineering 7%, biology 0%. DataVoyager (GPT-4p) 9.9% vs 17.5% on archaeology tasks with domain-knowledge hints (text wording in paper is ambiguous about which is which; read as 9.9% without, 17.5% with). Workflow types: spatial analysis 0%, pollen dating 0%, ecological modelling 0%.
limits: Replicating a paper's workflow took up to 90 person-hours per dataset and 30% of attempts failed. Scoring by LLM judge.
agent_relevance: Domain knowledge hint helps; hard statistical workflows fail. Argues for tool-backed analysis steps and not just reasoning.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: a virtual environment for developing and evaluating automated scientific discovery agents
finding: Full discovery cycles (hypothesise, experiment, analyse, act) in simulated worlds with 120 tasks. Baseline LLM agents did far worse than 11 human scientists.
numbers: Humans: 66% average task completion, 55% knowledge score. Best agent (ReAct) completed 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks; best explanatory agent (Hypothesizer) found 34% of gold knowledge on easy, 8% on challenge. Unit-test sub-skills about 60%+.
limits: Simplified worlds; human N=11; agents were generic baselines.
agent_relevance: Agents fail at the loop, not at single steps. Supports a program-controlled loop with a running check.

source: Lu, Lu, Lange, Foerster, Clune, Ha (2024) The AI Scientist: towards fully automated open-ended scientific discovery
finding: End-to-end agent: idea, novelty check by literature search, code experiments, write-up, automated review. Papers cost under $15 each. Claude Sonnet 3.5 gave the best yield.
numbers: Diffusion template: Sonnet 3.5 made 51 ideas, 49 judged novel, 38 passed experiments, 38 papers, mean reviewer score 3.82, max 6.0, cost $250; GPT-4o 16 papers, 3.70; DeepSeek Coder 31 papers, 3.32; Llama-3.1 405b 21 papers, 2.30. Automated reviewer: balanced accuracy 0.65 vs 0.66 for humans, F1 0.57 vs 0.49 on ICLR 2022 data.
limits: Authors list hallucinated results, LaTeX failures, invented hardware. Reviewer is an LLM, so scores are the system's own yardstick.
agent_relevance: The template for a running loop. Its own judge is an LLM, which G8 says not to trust for novelty.

source: Beel, Kan, Baumgart (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist: wishful thinking or an emerging reality
finding: Independent test of the AI Scientist found weak novelty checking (keyword search), many failed runs and hallucinated numbers.
numbers: 5 of 12 experiments (42%) failed from coding errors; each code iteration added only 8% more characters; median 5 citations per paper, 5 of 34 citations from 2020 or later; 4 of 7 manuscripts (57%) had missing figures or hallucinated numbers; cost $6-15 per paper plus 3.5 human hours; micro-batching for SGD labelled novel; its reviewer rejected 9 of 10 papers in one check.
limits: Small sample (12 ideas, 7 manuscripts); one older model version.
agent_relevance: Failed-replication data: LLM-judged novelty is unreliable (G8), and a loop without output checks yields fabricated results (G2, G3).

source: Yamada et al. (2025) The AI Scientist-v2: workshop-level automated scientific discovery via agentic tree search
finding: Dropped human code templates, added agentic tree search over experiments and a VLM figure check. Three fully AI papers were submitted blind to an ICLR workshop; one passed the human average acceptance threshold.
numbers: 3 papers submitted; best average reviewer score 6.33 (roughly top 45% of submissions); it would have been accepted after meta-review
limits: One workshop, N=3, workshop bar is low; authors withdrew the paper; the accepted paper's own result was a negative finding about a regulariser.
agent_relevance: Tree search with a check at each node is a working shape for open mode, but one success in three is not a rate.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2025) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Blind expert review of 49 ideas per condition. LLM ideas (after over-generate and rerank) were rated more novel than expert ideas, slightly weaker on feasibility.
numbers: 79 expert reviewers, 298 reviews. Novelty: human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI+human rerank 5.81 (p<0.05). Of 4000 seed ideas per topic only about 200 non-duplicates (cosine > 0.8 = duplicate). Inter-reviewer agreement 56.1%. LLM judges: GPT-4o direct 50.0, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7, Claude-3.5 pairwise 53.3, AI Scientist reviewer 43.3.
limits: Ideas only, not executed; 7 NLP topics; style normalised by an LLM rewrite.
agent_relevance: LLM judges are near chance for ranking ideas, so selection must come from running. Generation saturates, so diversity must be forced.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The ideation-execution gap: execution outcomes of LLM-generated versus human research ideas
finding: 43 experts executed randomly assigned ideas. The AI advantage seen at ideation vanished after execution; AI ideas lost more score on every metric.
numbers: Ideation: novelty human 4.912 vs AI 5.778; overall 4.596 vs 5.382. After execution: novelty 4.903 vs 4.729; overall 3.968 vs 3.406. Gap (execution minus ideation) AI vs human: novelty -1.049 vs -0.010, excitement -1.760 vs 0.078, effectiveness -1.879 vs -0.052, overall -1.976 vs -0.628. FDR p = 0.025, 0.001, 0.003, 0.004. N=19 human ideas, 24 AI ideas.
limits: Small N, one field, low statistical power for post-execution scores alone.
agent_relevance: Key result for G8: scoring ideas without running them inflates AI ideas by about 1-2 points. A running check is the correction.

source: Wang et al. (2024) SciMON: scientific inspiration machines optimized for novelty
finding: Retrieves 'inspirations' from literature and iteratively rewrites ideas until they are not too similar to related work. Iteration raised novelty, but generated ideas stayed far below the real paper ideas.
numbers: Ground-truth idea judged higher in technical depth and novelty in 85% of comparisons vs the best GPT-4 variant (GPT4FS+KG). Iterative novelty boost: first iteration gained novelty on 56% of updated ideas, second on 57.8%. KG variant higher technical detail in 48% of pairs, less incremental in 45%.
limits: Human evaluation of a small set; novelty defined against retrieved neighbours only.
agent_relevance: Similarity-to-prior-work as a code-computed novelty check (embedding distance) is a usable running check; models still lag human ideas.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Hypothesis generation with large language models (HypoGeniC)
finding: Generates hypotheses from data, then keeps a bank updated with a reward based on how often each hypothesis predicts new examples correctly (UCB-style). Hypotheses then drive classification.
numbers: Over few-shot in-context learning: +31.7% (shoe sales), +13.9% (deceptive reviews), +3.3% (headline popularity), +24.9% (tweet popularity). Updating the bank adds on average 0.7%, 5.8%, 8.1%, 7% by dataset. Beat supervised learning by 12.1% and 11.6% on two datasets.
limits: Gains on tweet data inflated because safety mode triggered in zero-shot for some models; four tasks.
agent_relevance: A running check on held-out examples with a code-side reward is the inner loop we want. Bank update helped but modestly.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Large language models for automated open-domain scientific hypotheses discovery (MOOSE)
finding: Multi-module framework with feedback loops generates hypotheses from raw web data with a background and an inspiration. Tested whether hypotheses were new to the model's training window and valid.
numbers: Not extracted this session beyond abstract-level claims; see paper for expert-rated validity and novelty tables
limits: Fetched only the text; numbers not verified here, treat as unread detail.
agent_relevance: Early example of feedback modules inside a hypothesis loop; low confidence entry.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Towards an AI co-scientist (Google)
finding: Multi-agent system with generate, debate, rank (Elo tournament), evolve. Elo rose with more compute and no saturation up to the test limit. Experts preferred its outputs on 11 research goals.
numbers: 203 research goals for Elo trend; expert-rated 11 goals: mean preference rank 2.36, novelty 3.64 and impact 3.09 out of 5. AML drug repurposing: IC50 as low as 2 nM across all AML cell lines tested. Elo vs GPQA accuracy concordance tested against Gemini 2.0 reference with 32 samples per question.
limits: Elo is an auto-evaluation by the system's own judge; paper states expert evaluations are subjective; wet-lab validation on a few cases chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: Tournament-ranked self-play helps in their data, but ranking is by LLM, which conflicts with G5; wet-lab/test result is the only true check.

source: Gupta, Pruthi (2025) All that glitters is not novel: plagiarism in AI generated research
finding: 13 experts searching for overlap with existing work found a quarter of LLM research proposals were paraphrased or heavily borrowed. Automated plagiarism detectors missed them.
numbers: 24.0% of 50 documents verified plagiarised (cross-checked by source authors); remaining 76% had partial similarity; plagiarism rate among human papers far lower; best automated detector 88.8% accuracy only on oracle conditions
limits: 50 documents, from four systems incl. AI Scientist; experts primed to search for plagiarism.
agent_relevance: A novelty check must be a search against prior work in code, and results of novelty ratings by blind reviewers (c13) may be inflated by this.

source: Novikov et al. (2025) AlphaEvolve: a coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery
finding: LLM-proposed program edits are scored by automatic evaluators and evolved. Matches or beats best-known constructions on many open maths problems.
numbers: Over 50 open problems: matched best known on 75%, surpassed on 20%. Kissing number in 11 dimensions raised to 593. Tensor decomposition: of 54 targets, matches SOTA in 38, surpasses in 14, falls behind in 2.
limits: Only problems with an automatic score function; results by authors; 'likely already optimal' for many matches.
agent_relevance: Best-case evidence: a free, exact running check turns an LLM proposer into a discoverer. The check is the lever, not the model's reasoning.

source: Mitchener et al. (2025) Kosmos: an AI scientist for autonomous discovery
finding: Long-run agent with structured world model reads papers and runs code over cycles. Every statement is cited to code or literature. Independent scientists audited the statements.
numbers: 79.4% of statements accurate overall: 85.5% data-analysis, 82.1% literature, 57.9% synthesis/interpretation. Up to 200 rollouts, about 42,000 lines of code and 1,500 papers per run; 7 highlighted discoveries, 3 reproduced preprints not seen at runtime; collaborators reported value scaling linearly to 20 cycles.
limits: Accuracy audit does not test whether chosen analyses were important; 'six months of work' is collaborator self-report.
agent_relevance: Where a model interprets, accuracy drops by about 25 points compared with code-grounded statements. Keep interpretation separate from run-backed claims.

source: Ghareeb et al. (2025) Robin: a multi-agent system for automating scientific discovery
finding: Agents propose hypotheses, humans run lab assays, agents analyse results and propose follow-ups. For dry AMD it identified ripasudil, a ROCK inhibitor not before proposed for the disease, and validated increased RPE phagocytosis.
numbers: Single case study; one drug candidate validated in vitro; follow-up RNA-seq analysis proposed by the system
limits: One disease; lab steps by humans; no rate of failed candidates reported in the part read.
agent_relevance: Shows the loop with real-world check can close; evidence is a single success.

source: Baek et al. (2024) ResearchAgent: iterative research idea generation over scientific literature with LLMs
finding: Iterative idea generation with entity-augmented literature and reviewing agents that give feedback by human-derived criteria. Evaluated with human and model judges, which agree.
numbers: Agreement between human annotators and model-based evaluation reported via Spearman and Cohen's kappa (Table 1); exact values not extracted here
limits: Judges include an LLM; no execution.
agent_relevance: Reviewer-agent feedback loop without a run; subject to the ideation-execution gap in c14.

source: Li et al. (2024) Chain of Ideas: revolutionizing research via novel idea development with LLM agents
finding: Organises literature as a chain of progressive developments so the LLM sees the trend before proposing. Uses an arena-style (Idea Arena) pairwise evaluation said to agree with humans, and claims quality comparable to humans.
numbers: Minimum cost $0.50 per candidate idea and experiment design; agreement numbers not extracted here
limits: Evaluation is LLM-judged pairwise, the style c13 found near chance for experts' rank.
agent_relevance: Structuring prior work as a trajectory is a cheap prompt scaffold; its benefit is not confirmed by execution.

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench: evaluating AI's ability to replicate AI research
finding: Agents must reproduce 20 ICML 2024 papers from scratch, graded on rubrics co-written with authors. Best agent scored 21.0%. ML PhDs scored higher on a subset.
numbers: 20 papers, 8,316 gradable outcomes; Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) 21.0%; 3-paper subset: humans 41.4% (best of 3, 48 hours) vs o1 26.6%; Code-Dev variant o1 43.4%
limits: Replication is not discovery; LLM judge used for grading, validated against human grades.
agent_relevance: Even recipe-following research loops fall short; discovery in open mode is harder.

source: Vafa, Chang, Rambachan, Mullainathan (2025) What has a foundation model found? Using inductive bias to probe for world models
finding: A sequence model trained on orbital trajectories predicts orbits very well but, when fine-tuned for force vectors, does not behave as if it learned Newton's law. Symbolic regression on its implied force recovers a nonsensical law.
numbers: R2 above 0.9999 on trajectory prediction; inconsistent implied force laws across data slices
limits: Trained transformers, not LLM agents; synthetic orbit data.
agent_relevance: Good prediction does not mean a law was found. A discovery loop needs a test on new tasks (G3), the Kepler to Newton jump, which BACON never needed to make.

source: Derived contrast of Si et al. (2025) ideation study and ideation-execution gap study (c13, c14)
finding: Across studies, idea-stage ratings favour AI ideas, while post-execution ratings and audits favour humans or erase the gap. Seen in c13 vs c14, c11, c19.
numbers: Gap: AI minus human overall score +0.79 at ideation (5.382 vs 4.596); -0.56 after execution (3.406 vs 3.968)
limits: Computed by me from c14 Table 4 means; N=19 and 24 ideas.
agent_relevance: Strongest single design rule for open mode: never let unrun judgement end the loop.

source: Philosophy-of-science critique of BACON (Springer chapter; author unverified)
finding: A critique argues BACON's evaluation rests on two historical case studies (sine law of refraction, Kepler's third law) and cannot show an adequate general model of discovery.
numbers: 2 case studies; no measured rates
limits: Seen only as a search snippet; author and details unverified.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: BACON succeeded where variables were given and the law was a simple power relation. Open mode should not assume that holds.
